paper_context.research_question: Can convolutional neural networks automatically learn useful cognitive features from readers' eye‑movement (gaze) data, and does combining these learned gaze features with learned text features improve performance on sentiment polarity and sarcasm detection compared to (a) text‑only CNNs and (b) existing systems that use handcrafted gaze and textual features?
contribution_type: algorithmic application/architecture (multimodal CNN integrating text and gaze)
empirical evaluation on existing datasets enriched with eye‑tracking
main_claims: A CNN architecture that jointly learns features from text and eye‑movement (fixation and saccade) channels yields better classification performance for sentiment polarity and sarcasm detection than (i) CNNs using text alone and (ii) prior systems that use handcrafted gaze and textual features, on at least one publicly available dataset.

Automatically learned gaze features provide complementary information to textual features: incorporating gaze consistently improves CNN performance over text‑only CNN variants (statistically significant in some cases).

The learned multimodal feature representations exhibit distinguishable patterns for sarcastic versus non‑sarcastic instances (visualized differences in merged hidden representations), suggesting the model captures cognitive signals related to linguistic subtleties.
The benefit of the approach depends on dataset characteristics (e.g., dataset 2 shows CNNs do not outperform handcrafted features overall, though adding gaze still helps relative to text‑only CNNs).
expected_evaluation_dimensions: classification performance (precision/recall/F1) on sentiment polarity and sarcasm detection tasks
statistical significance of performance differences (e.g., McNemar test reported for some comparisons)
comparison across model variants (text‑only vs gaze‑only vs combined; static/nonstatic/multichannel embeddings; fixation vs saccade vs multichannel gaze)
robustness/generalization across datasets (two public datasets with different reader counts and characteristics)
ablation/analysis of learned representations (qualitative visualization and interpretation of hidden layer activations)
training behavior and overfitting indications (e.g., training convergence, validation stability, dataset size effects)
sensitivity to hyperparameters (embedding dimension, filter sizes, regularization) and practical scalability (ordering constraint on gaze participant rows)

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that (1) convolutional neural networks can automatically learn useful features from readers' eye-movement (gaze) data, (2) combining those learned gaze features with learned text features improves binary sentiment polarity and sarcasm classification relative to text-only CNNs and prior handcrafted-feature systems on at least one dataset, and (3) merged hidden-layer activations qualitatively exhibit patterns that correspond to sarcasm vs non-sarcasm. The structure: motivation (eye-movement correlates with linguistic subtleties) → method (two-component CNN: text per Kim 2014, gaze as P×G 2D convolutions with FIXATION/SACCADE/MULTICHANNEL variants) → experiments (two public datasets with 7 and 5 readers; many CNN variants; hyperparameters fixed by trial-and-error) → results (Tables 1–2: improvements on dataset1 vs Mishra et al.; mixed results on dataset2; qualitative visualization of 150-d merge-layer activations) → discussion and limitations (dataset dependence, overfitting on dataset2) → conclusions. The reasoning chain connects biological plausibility and prior handcrafted gaze work to an NN-based feature-learning approach, then to empirical evaluation. Strengths are concrete (explicit CNN design, many ablations of channel variants, replication of prior 10-fold splits). Weak points in the chain: statistical testing and experimental-control details are sparse (McNemar reported but without contingency tables or multiple-comparison correction); gaze preprocessing, participant-order dependency, and normalization choices are critical assumptions that are not thoroughly tested; qualitative interpretability claims lack quantitative separability analyses and may be confounded by lexical cues; hyperparameter selection and baseline tuning are not systematically documented, leaving possible alternative explanations for some performance differences. The paper's core empirical claim (improvement on dataset1) is supported by reported F-scores and a stated significance test, but reproducibility checks (exact splits, preprocessing scripts, and full test-prediction records) are needed to resolve uncertainty. The visualization evidence is hypothesis-generating but insufficient to demonstrate that learned activations capture cognitive signals rather than lexical or length artifacts.
logical_argument_graph: A1 Motivation: Linguistic subtleties (surprisal/cognitive load) correlate with gaze signals (fixations/saccades) → therefore gaze may provide complementary features for NLP tasks (§2).
A2 Limitation of prior work: Existing cognitive-NLP systems use handcrafted gaze features which may miss latent signals → motivates automated feature learning (§1, related work).

A3 Method proposition: Use a multimodal CNN with separate text and gaze components (text: 1D conv channels per Kim 2014; gaze: P×G 2D convs over FIXATION/SACCADE channels) to learn features jointly (§4).

A4 Design assumptions: Preprocessing (min-max normalization of fixation durations), fixed participant row ordering, and hyperparameter choices provide valid input representations and fair comparisons (§4.2, §5).

A5 Empirical test: Evaluate many variants (static/non-static/multichannel text; fixation/saccade/multichannel gaze; combined variants) on two public datasets using same 10-fold splits as prior work (§5).

A6 Key empirical claim: On dataset1, combined text+gaze CNN variants outperform prior handcrafted systems (Mishra et al.) and text-only CNNs; some differences reported as statistically significant (Table 1, §6.1).
A7 Caveat: On dataset2, CNNs underperform handcrafted-feature systems though adding gaze still improves over text-only CNNs; training behaviour indicates possible overfitting (§6.1).

A8 Interpretation claim: Visualizations of merged hidden-layer activations show differences between sarcastic and non-sarcastic examples when gaze is included, suggesting cognitive-signal capture (§7, Figure 4).
A9 Conclusions & future work: The approach is promising for cognitive-NLP; further hyperparameter tuning, representation alternatives, and broader tasks should be explored (§9).

concerns.title: Incomplete statistical testing and reporting
concerns.description: The paper reports p < 0.05 via McNemar for some comparisons but does not provide contingency tables, exact p-values, number of comparisons, or corrections for multiple hypothesis testing; this undermines confidence in claimed statistical significance.
evidence: §6.1: '... maximum F-score improvement of 3.8%. This improvement is statistically significant of p < 0.05 as confirmed by McNemar test.' No further test details provided.
Shared uncertainty flags note missing contingency table and multiple comparisons concerns.

concerns.title: Participant-order dependency not addressed
concerns.description: Gaze P×G representation is sensitive to the ordering of participant rows; authors keep a fixed ordering for scalability but do not test whether ordering introduces spurious signals or biases classification.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a multimodal CNN that learns features from text and per-snippet multi-reader gaze inputs (fixation durations and fixation positions) represented as P×G matrices. The architecture applies 1D convolutions over text (Kim-style static/non-static channels) and 2D convolutions over the gaze matrices (per-participant rows × sequence columns), merges pooled features into a 150-unit MLP and predicts sentiment/sarcasm labels. Experiments on two public gaze-enriched datasets (dataset1: 994 snippets, P=7; dataset2: 843 snippets, P=5) compare text-only, gaze-only and combined variants, and report that (a) combined text+gaze CNNs outperform text-only CNNs consistently and (b) on dataset1 combined CNNs beat prior handcrafted text+gaze systems (max F improvement 3.8%, McNemar p<0.05). Qualitative visualizations of merged hidden activations are used to argue that multimodal features separate sarcastic/non-sarcastic instances. The reported limitations include dataset dependence (CNNs underperform handcrafted systems on dataset2) and acknowledged sensitivity to hyperparameters, embedding dimension, and participant row ordering. Key methodological gaps concern statistical test details, reproducibility artifacts (split indices, preprocessing, gaze normalization), limited ablations (ordering/permutation invariance, normalization alternatives, cross-subject generalization), and qualitative-only interpretability claims.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper advances the idea that cognitive signals from readers' eye movements (fixations and saccades) can be automatically encoded by convolutional neural networks and combined with learned text embeddings to improve binary sentiment and sarcasm classification. The authors operationalize gaze as P×G matrices (participants × sequence length) with separate channels for fixation duration and fixation position, apply 2D convolutions over these matrices (and 1D convolutions over word-embedding sequences following Kim 2014), merge pooled features from text and gaze branches into a 150-unit fully connected layer, and train end-to-end. Experiments on two public gaze-enriched datasets compare text-only CNNs, gaze-only CNNs, combined CNNs, and previously published handcrafted-feature systems. Key empirical outcomes: combined text+gaze CNNs outperform prior handcrafted systems on dataset1 (statistically significant by reported McNemar test) and consistently beat text-only CNN variants; on dataset2, CNNs do not beat the handcrafted baseline though adding gaze still helps versus text-only CNNs; learned merge-layer activations are visualized to qualitatively argue that multimodal features capture finer distinctions (e.g., sarcasm intensity). The authors acknowledge limitations (dataset dependence, potential overfitting on dataset2, order-sensitivity of gaze encoding) and propose future ablations and hyperparameter optimization.
logical_argument_graph: L1: Linguistic subtleties (sarcasm, irony) induce measurable eye-movement phenomena (fixation durations, irregular saccades) — supported by cognitive literature and prior gaze-NLP work.
L2: Prior gaze-based NLP relied on handcrafted features that may miss subtle, high-dimensional patterns.

L3: Convolutional neural networks can learn hierarchical filters from raw signals (successful in images/text) and thus can be applied to gaze time/position matrices to automatically learn cognitive features.
L4: Represent gaze as P×G matrices with fixation-duration and fixation-position channels; apply 2D convolutions to capture cross-participant and temporal/spatial gaze patterns.
L5: Combine learned gaze features with a Kim-style text-CNN via a merged fully-connected layer to enable complementary multimodal representations.
L6: Evaluate on two public datasets using identical 10-fold splits and compare to text-only CNNs and previously published handcrafted-feature systems.

L7: Empirical findings: (a) On dataset1, combined CNN outperforms prior handcrafted systems (claimed significant); (b) combining gaze consistently improves over text-only CNNs across variants; (c) dataset2 shows CNN overfitting and handcrafted features still better overall; (d) merge-layer visualizations show qualitative differences between sarcastic and non-sarcastic examples.

L8: Conclusion: learned gaze features provide complementary cognitive signal and automatic feature learning is promising, but benefits depend on dataset characteristics and representation/training choices.

Architecture reuses established text-CNN patterns (Kim 2014) but augments with a novel gaze branch.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: Reconstructed reasoning: (1) Cognitive signals in eye-movements (fixations/saccades) reflect linguistic surprisal and cognitive load that are informative for subtle textual phenomena (sarcasm, nuanced sentiment). (2) Prior cognitive-NLP work used handcrafted gaze features; manual design may miss patterns. (3) Convolutional networks can learn local spatio-temporal filters; apply 1D CNN for text and 2D CNN over P×G gaze matrices to automatically learn cognitive features, then merge learned text and gaze representations. (4) Train multiple variants (static/non-static/multichannel text × fixation/saccade/multichannel gaze) and compare to text-only CNNs and published handcrafted-feature systems on two public datasets using the same 10-fold splits. (5) On dataset1 the combined multimodal CNNs improve F-scores over prior handcrafted systems and over text-only CNNs (statistical test claimed). (6) On dataset2 CNNs underperform handcrafted features but adding gaze still improves text-only CNNs; training dynamics suggest overfitting. (7) Qualitative merge-layer visualizations show distinguishable activation patterns for sarcastic vs non-sarcastic examples, interpreted as the model capturing cognitive distinctions. (8) Conclude that automatically learned gaze features complement text features and that the approach is promising but dataset-dependent.
logical_argument_graph: A1 (eye-movements reflect cognitive response to linguistic subtleties) -> motivates adding gaze signals to text models.
Observation: manual gaze features are limited -> leads to hypothesis that learned features might capture richer signals.
Design: adopt CNN text component (Kim 2014) + 2D CNN over P×G gaze matrices -> architecture claimed to learn complementary features.
Empirical test: train multiple variants on two datasets using 10-fold splits -> compare to text-only CNNs and Mishra et al. baselines.
Result: dataset1: multimodal CNN > handcrafted baseline and text-only CNN (F improvement up to 3.8%, p<0.05); dataset2: multimodal helps relative to text-only but not vs handcrafted.
Interpretation: learned gaze features are complementary; visualization of merge layer shows activation differences between sarcastic and non-sarcastic examples.
Caveat: dataset dependence and methodological assumptions (normalization, participant ordering, hyperparameter choices) may limit generalizability.

identified_claims.claim_label: multimodal CNN improves over prior handcrafted systems (dataset1)
identified_claims.claim_text: On dataset 1 (Mishra et al. 2016a), CNN variants that jointly learn from text and gaze outperform the best previously published systems that use handcrafted text and gaze features, with a maximum F-score improvement of 3.8% (statistically significant, p < 0.05 by McNemar test).
evidence: Table 1: MULTICHANNELTEXT + MULTICHANNELGAZE F=76.24 vs prior 'Text + Gaze (Best)'=73.5 (shared_analysis/extracted_claims).
§6.1: explicit statement that improvement is statistically significant (McNemar test, p<0.05).
uncertainty_flags: Details of contingency counts and exact McNemar application not provided; possible split/preprocessing differences with Mishra et al. could affect comparability.
Hyperparameter tuning and model selection procedures for baselines vs proposed models not fully detailed.

identified_claims.claim_label: gaze adds complementary information to text CNNs
identified_claims.claim_text: Across datasets and model variants, incorporating learned gaze features into the CNN consistently improves performance over text-only CNN variants (e.g., ~5% F-score improvement on dataset1; smaller but consistent improvements on dataset2).
evidence: Table 1: MULTICHANNELTEXT F=71.53 vs with gaze MULTICHANNELTEXT + MULTICHANNELGAZE F=76.24 (dataset1).
§6.1: 'we observe an F-score improvement of around 5% for CNNs with both gaze and text components ... statistically significant'.
Table 1 (dataset2): text-only ~60 F vs text+gaze variants ~62–64 F (smaller gains).
uncertainty_flags: On dataset2 combined CNNs still fall short of handcrafted-feature systems; 'across datasets' statement is qualified and not uniformly supported.
Some improvements are small and reported significance not uniformly shown.

identified_claims.claim_label: multimodal representations exhibit distinguishable patterns for sarcasm
identified_claims.claim_text: Learned multimodal feature representations (merged hidden-layer activations) show distinguishable visual patterns between sarcastic and non-sarcastic instances, suggesting the model captures cognitive signals related to linguistic subtleties.
evidence: Figure 4: color-bar visualizations of 150-dim merge-layer outputs for four examples; authors note intensified patterns for sarcastic example.
§7: narrative connecting higher intensity in some features with sarcasm.
uncertainty_flags: Evidence is qualitative and based on a few examples; no quantitative separability metrics (e.g., clustering, classification on activations) or controls for lexical confounds provided.
Visual differences could be due to vocabulary, length, or dataset artifacts rather than cognitive signal capture.

identified_claims.claim_label: dataset dependence of benefits
identified_claims.claim_text: The benefit of the approach depends on dataset characteristics: on dataset 2 CNNs do not outperform handcrafted-feature systems overall (though adding gaze improves text-only CNNs), and there are overfitting indications (training accuracy reaches 100% within 25 epochs on dataset2).
evidence: Table 1: prior 'Text + Gaze (Best)' on dataset2 = 71.8 vs proposed CNN best ~64.29 F.
§6.1: 'training accuracy reaches 100 within 25 epochs with validation accuracy stable around 50%', suggesting overfitting.
uncertainty_flags: Overfitting claim is plausible but not supported by plotted learning curves or systematic regularization/ablation to confirm cause.
Dataset characteristics (reader behavior, text source, labeling differences) are not quantitatively analyzed.

identified_claims.claim_label: gaze-only CNNs yield nontrivial performance
identified_claims.claim_text: CNNs trained only on gaze channels (FIXATION, SACCADE, MULTICHANNELGAZE) achieve nontrivial classification performance, indicating that gaze signal alone carries task-relevant information.
evidence: Table 1: FIXATION F≈59.54, SACCADE F≈62.32, MULTICHANNELGAZE F≈62.68 (dataset1).
Table 2 (sarcasm): FIXATION F≈71.93, SACCADE F≈68.40, MULTICHANNELGAZE F≈67.82.
uncertainty_flags: Absolute accuracy lower than combined models; no statistical or baseline comparisons (random/majority) reported for gaze-only variants.
Performance may be dataset-specific and sensitive to small participant counts.

strengths.title: Novel multimodal framing that delegates cognitive feature engineering to learning
strengths.description: The paper proposes treating gaze as a learned multimodal input rather than relying on handcrafted gaze features, framing cognitive feature extraction as an end-to-end learning problem.
evidence: Introduction contrasts handcrafted gaze features (Mishra et al.) with proposed learned features via CNN; §4 describes joint CNN architecture for text and gaze.

strengths.title: Concrete architectural instantiation bridging text and gaze
strengths.description: Provides a concrete model design (1D text CNN + 2D gaze CNN over P×G matrices, merge-layer) that others can build on or adapt for different gaze encodings.
evidence: §4.1 and §4.2 detail text and gaze components, including filter shapes, pooling, and merge-layer design; Figure 3 shows full architecture.

strengths.title: Empirical improvement on at least one public dataset
strengths.description: Demonstrates measurable F-score gains vs prior handcrafted-feature systems on dataset1, with a reported significance claim.
evidence: Table 1 and §6.1: maximum F improvement of 3.8% over Mishra et al., p<0.05 (McNemar test) reported.

strengths.title: Honest discussion of limitations and dataset dependence
strengths.description: Authors explicitly acknowledge dataset dependence, overfitting on dataset2, and discuss effects of embedding dims and channel choices.
evidence: §6.1 and §7 contain discussion on dataset2 underperformance, overfitting signs, and channel-specific observations (fixation vs saccade).

concerns.title: Incomplete statistical testing details
concerns.description: Statistical significance claims (McNemar p<0.05) are stated but contingency tables, exact counts, and corrections for multiple comparisons are not reported, making verification impossible.
evidence: §6.1: 'This improvement is statistically significant of p < 0.05 as confirmed by McNemar test.' No further test details given in the manuscript or tables.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide full McNemar contingency tables (pairwise predictions on identical test folds), report exact p-values, and apply multiple-comparison corrections (e.g., Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg) when many pairwise tests are run.

concerns.title: Participant-ordering confound in P×G gaze matrices
concerns.description: Gaze component is order-sensitive (row order of participants kept constant). If row ordering correlates with labels or reader traits, the model might learn ordering artifacts rather than cognitive signals.
evidence: §4.2 explicitly states the gaze P×G matrix is not permutation-invariant and the authors keep the order constant for scalability reasons.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run ablations: (a) randomize participant row order at training and test to check sensitivity; (b) use permutation-invariant aggregations (mean/max across participants) or attention/learned pooling; (c) report leave-one-reader-out experiments to assess cross-subject generalization.

concerns.title: Limited exploration of gaze preprocessing and normalization choices
concerns.description: Gaze channels use min-max normalization across participants and fixed encodings for saccades; alternative normalization (z-score, per-snippet scaling) or encodings (time-series alignment, per-word aggregation) are not explored and could substantially affect learned features.
evidence: §4.2: 'scaled across participants using min-max normalization to reduce subjectivity.' No comparative preprocessing experiments reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include experiments comparing normalization strategies (min-max vs z-score vs per-snippet scaling), different saccade encodings (direction/length vs word-id sequences), and justify chosen pipeline with ablation results.

concerns.title: Small per-snippet reader counts threaten generalization
concerns.description: Datasets have P=7 and P=5 readers per snippet; small participant pools increase risk of models learning idiosyncratic reader patterns and prevent assessing cross-subject generalization.
evidence: §5 Dataset description: 7 readers for dataset1, 5 for dataset2; shared_analysis flagged overfitting and need for leave-one-reader-out tests.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate cross-reader generalization using leave-one-reader-out or test-on-held-out-readers protocols; report variability across reader subsets and aggregate metrics with confidence intervals.

concerns.title: Qualitative interpretability claims lack quantitative support
concerns.description: Claim that merge-layer activations capture cognitive distinctions (e.g., sarcasm intensity) rests on a few illustrative visualizations; quantitative separability tests and checks for lexical confounds are absent.
evidence: §7 and Figure 4 show color-bar plots for four examples and interpret intensity differences, but no separability metrics or confound analyses are provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute quantitative analyses on merge-layer vectors: clustering metrics (silhouette, ARI), classification accuracy using only merged activations, and controls that remove top lexical cues to test whether activations correlate with vocabulary rather than gaze.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter selection and baseline parity not fully documented
concerns.description: Hyperparameters were set by 'trial and error' and no systematic tuning is reported; unclear whether baselines (text-only CNN, Mishra et al.) received equivalent tuning, raising fairness concerns.
evidence: §5: 'These model hyper-parameters are fixed by trial and error ... tuning might help' ; shared_analysis notes hyperparameter sensitivity and possible unfair comparisons.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report hyperparameter search ranges and procedures; ensure baselines are tuned comparably or run controlled comparisons with identical tuning budgets, and release scripts used for model selection.

concerns.title: Scalability/permutation tradeoff left unresolved
concerns.description: Authors acknowledge that making the gaze model permutation-invariant would require training on permutations (infeasible), but do not explore scalable alternatives (attention across participants, symmetric functions).
evidence: §4.2 paragraph noting permutation issue and rejecting exhaustive permutations for scalability reasons.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Experiment with permutation-robust architectures: participant-wise CNN followed by symmetric pooling (mean/max), set/DeepSets layers, or learned attention over participants to achieve invariance without factorial complexity.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a multimodal CNN that jointly learns features from text and multi-reader gaze inputs (fixation durations and fixation positions encoded as P×G matrices) and evaluates many variants (static/non-static/multichannel text × fixation/saccade/multichannel gaze) on two public gaze-enriched datasets for sentiment polarity and sarcasm detection. Main empirical claims are: (1) combined text+gaze CNNs outperform text-only CNNs and beat prior handcrafted text+gaze systems on dataset1 (max +3.8% F, reported McNemar p<0.05); (2) adding gaze consistently improves text-only CNNs across variants/datasets though gains vary and sometimes are not significant; (3) learned merged hidden representations visually differ for sarcastic vs non-sarcastic examples; (4) benefits are dataset-dependent (dataset2 shows CNNs underperform handcrafted systems and overfitting signs). The empirical evidence in the manuscript (Tables 1–2, textual reporting of significance tests, Figure 4 visualizations) supports the existence of performance gains on dataset1 and relative gains of combined vs text-only CNNs. However, statistical reporting is sparse (no contingency tables, unclear multiple-comparisons control) and key methodological choices (gaze normalization, fixed participant row ordering, limited reader counts, hyperparameter tuning procedure, fairness of baseline tuning) create nontrivial uncertainty about internal validity and generalizability. The interpretability claim (visualized activation patterns) is qualitative and underpowered without quantitative separability or confound controls. Overall, the paper presents promising evidence that CNNs can learn useful features from gaze that complement text features, but several experiments and reporting improvements are necessary to substantiate robustness and rule out confounds.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Linguistic subtleties map to cognitive signals (prior literature and Mishra et al.) -> motivates use of gaze.
A2: Handcrafted gaze features may miss patterns -> motivates automatic feature learning via CNN.
Design: Encode text via Kim (2014)-style CNN; encode gaze as P×G matrices with 2D convolutions (fixation/saccade channels); merge pooled representations into 150-d hidden layer -> classifier.
Experiment: Evaluate on two public datasets (dataset1 P=7 readers, dataset2 P=5 readers), compare text-only, gaze-only, and combined models, and compare to prior handcrafted-feature systems.
Observation 1: On dataset1 combined CNN variants beat prior systems (max +3.8% F) and beat text-only CNNs (~5% F gain); McNemar reported p<0.05.

Observation 2: On dataset2 CNNs do not beat handcrafted baseline though combined still outperforms text-only CNNs (smaller gains); training accuracy reaches 100% quickly indicating probable overfitting.
Observation 3: Gaze-only models achieve nontrivial F-scores but below combined models (Tables 1–2).
Interpretation: Gaze provides complementary cognitive signal; multimodal CNN can learn such features; benefits are dataset-dependent and sensitive to data size and preprocessing.
Weak links: statistical-test reporting incomplete, participant-ordering dependency acknowledged but untested, normalization and representation choices not ablated, interpretability is qualitative.

No control analyses (e.g., remove top discriminative words, randomize gaze, or permutation tests) to rule out alternative explanations.

identified_claims.claim_label: dataset dependence of benefits
identified_claims.claim_text: The benefit of adding gaze and of the CNN architecture depends on dataset characteristics: on dataset 2 CNNs do not outperform handcrafted-feature systems overall (though adding gaze improves text-only CNNs), and there are overfitting indications (training accuracy reaches 100% within 25 epochs on dataset2).
evidence: §6.1: 'For dataset 2, CNN based approaches do not perform better than manual feature based approaches.'
Table 1: Mishra et al. Text + Gaze (Best) F=71.8 (dataset2) vs CNN variants top around 64.29 F.
§6.1: 'training accuracy reaches 100 within 25 epochs with validation accuracy stable around 50%, indicating the possibility of overfitting.'
uncertainty_flags: Authors hypothesize overfitting; full learning curves, loss traces, and cross-validation diagnostics are not provided to substantiate this claim.
Differences in dataset composition (tweet vs movie-review mix, label noise) not fully analyzed; thus cause of dataset-dependent performance is not rigorously established.

identified_claims.claim_label: gaze-only CNNs yield nontrivial performance
identified_claims.claim_text: CNNs trained only on gaze channels (FIXATION, SACCADE, MULTICHANNELGAZE) achieve nontrivial classification performance (e.g., fixation/saccade-only F-scores around 59–63 for sentiment; ~67–72 for sarcasm), indicating that gaze signal alone carries task-relevant information.
evidence: Table 1 (dataset1): FIXATION F=59.54, SACCADE F=62.32, MULTICHANNELGAZE F=62.68.
Table 2 (sarcasm): FIXATION F=71.93, SACCADE F=68.40, MULTICHANNELGAZE F=67.82.
uncertainty_flags: Gaze-only performance is lower than combined models; practical utility as standalone classifiers not demonstrated.
No statistical comparison to simple baselines (e.g., majority class, shuffled gaze) reported; possible that models exploit dataset artifacts or align with lexical cues via indirect correlations.

strengths.title: Well-motivated multimodal architecture
strengths.description: Combines established text CNN (Kim 2014 style) with a principled 2D convolutional treatment of multi-reader gaze matrices, enabling end-to-end learned cognitive features.
evidence: §3 and §4 describe the rationale for CNNs and the two-component architecture with text and gaze branches; Figure 3 illustrates the model.
Design includes multiple experimental variants (static/nonstatic/multichannel text × fixation/saccade/multichannel gaze).

strengths.title: Empirical evaluation on public gaze-enriched datasets
strengths.description: Uses two published datasets with available eye-tracking data, enabling direct comparison to prior handcrafted-feature systems and facilitating reproducibility if artifacts are released.
evidence: §5: Dataset descriptions: dataset1 (Mishra et al. 2016a) and dataset2 (Joshi et al. 2014) with P=7 and P=5 readers respectively; use of same 10-fold configuration claimed.
Tables 1–2 show per-variant precision/recall/F measures across both tasks.

strengths.title: Transparent acknowledgement of limitations
strengths.description: Authors explicitly note dataset-dependent performance, overfitting on dataset2, sensitivity to hyperparameters, and participant-ordering issues in gaze representation.
evidence: §6.1 mentions overfitting signs on dataset2; §4.2 acknowledges that P×G gaze input is not order-invariant and training uses constant ordering; §7 discusses hyperparameter and embedding-dimension effects.

strengths.title: Wide set of ablation-like variants tested
strengths.description: Paper reports many model variants (text-only, gaze-only, combined; static vs nonstatic embeddings; fixation vs saccade vs multichannel gaze), giving a richer empirical picture.
evidence: Tables 1–2 list ~15+ model configurations with per-variant P/R/F values enabling comparisons among component choices.

concerns.title: Insufficient statistical reporting for claimed significance
concerns.description: Significance claims (McNemar p<0.05) are stated but key details are missing: contingency tables or paired counts, which comparisons were tested, whether multiple comparisons were corrected, and raw prediction outputs for reproducibility.
evidence: §6.1 reports McNemar p<0.05 for dataset1 improvement but provides no contingency table or exact p-values.
Multiple pairwise comparisons across many model variants are reported without correction for multiple testing.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide full contingency tables (TP/FP counts for both classifiers) for reported McNemar tests, exact p-values, and indicate which pairwise comparisons were tested; apply and report multiple-comparison correction (e.g., Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg) or use a single primary comparison per claim.

concerns.title: Participant-row-ordering confound in gaze input encoding
concerns.description: Gaze P×G matrices are not permutation-invariant and authors keep a fixed ordering of participant rows; if ordering correlates with labels or participant characteristics, models may exploit ordering artifacts rather than genuine cognitive signals.
evidence: §4.2 explicitly acknowledges invariance issue and states they keep order constant for scalability.
No experiments reported that randomize or permute participant rows or use permutation-invariant pooling to test sensitivity.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run ablations where participant rows are permuted (random order per instance), and compare performance; alternatively implement permutation-invariant aggregation (e.g., per-word pooling across participants, attention across participants, or DeepSets-like processing) to check whether ordering is being exploited.

concerns.title: Limited validation of gaze preprocessing and normalization choices
concerns.description: Gaze inputs are min-max normalized across participants and encoded as fixation durations and word-id saccades; alternative normalizations (z-score), aggregations, or denoising strategies are not evaluated, leaving uncertainty about robustness of results to preprocessing.
evidence: §4.2 notes min-max normalization 'to reduce subjectivity' but no ablations comparing normalization methods are presented.
Assumptions list highlights risk that normalization/discarding absolute timing cues could affect discriminative signals.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report experiments comparing min-max vs z-score normalization, per-participant standardization, no normalization, and aggregated per-word gaze features (mean/median across participants) to show robustness; include a run where gaze is replaced with random noise to estimate chance-level impact.

concerns.title: Qualitative interpretability claims lack quantitative support
concerns.description: Visualizations showing merge-layer activations for a few examples are suggestive but do not quantify separability of sarcastic vs non-sarcastic instances; potential lexical confounds (dataset vocabulary differences) are acknowledged but not controlled for.
evidence: §7 and Figure 4 present color-bar visualizations for 4 examples and assert intensity differences with gaze added.
Authors note vocabulary separation in sarcasm dataset which could explain activation differences.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute quantitative separability metrics (e.g., silhouette, clustering purity, LDA/CCA projections) on merge-layer activations across the full test set; run control analyses removing top discriminative words or shuffling gaze to test whether separability persists; report correlations between activations and simple lexical features to check confounds.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter tuning and baseline parity unclear
concerns.description: Hyperparameters were chosen 'by trial and error' and fixed; it is unclear whether text-only baselines and prior handcrafted-feature baselines were tuned equivalently, which could bias reported comparative improvements.
evidence: §5 states hyper-parameters are fixed by trial and error and tuning might improve performance; text mentions best embedding dim=50 but no systematic tuning details.
Comparisons to Mishra et al. rely on following 'same 10-fold configuration' but no code or split indices provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide hyperparameter search logs or at minimum a sensitivity analysis (vary filter counts, dropout, learning rate, embedding dims) showing stability of results; apply same tuning effort to text-only baselines; release code, random seeds, and fold indices for exact replication.

concerns.title: Limited generalization tests for small reader counts
concerns.description: Datasets have few readers per snippet (P=5–7), raising the risk that models learn participant-specific idiosyncrasies rather than generalizable cognitive patterns; no leave-one-reader-out or cross-subject validation is reported.
evidence: §5 dataset descriptions: P=7 and P=5 readers; §4.2 acknowledges participant-order sensitivity.
Shared analysis suggests leave-one-reader-out and held-out-reader tests as key reproducibility steps that are not present.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run cross-subject generalization experiments: leave-one-reader-out and evaluate whether models trained on readers A..N-1 generalize to held-out reader; alternatively train on a subset of snippets/readers and test on unseen readers to quantify dependence on particular readers.

comparable_works.relevance: Directly comparable prior work using handcrafted gaze and textual features for sentiment and sarcasm tasks on same datasets.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Shares datasets and goal of leveraging gaze; differs in using handcrafted features vs this paper's learned CNN features; authors compare empirically and report outperforming on dataset1.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript references and repeated comparisons in §5, §6 and Tables 1–2

comparable_works.relevance: Architectural basis for the text component and key baseline for text-only comparisons.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Text branch follows Kim (2014) static/non-static/multichannel design; difference is addition of gaze branch (2D convolutions) and merging.
comparable_works.source_trace: §4.1 and multiple mentions in paper (references to Kim 2014)

comparable_works.relevance: Other recent cognitive-NLP uses of gaze for tasks (sentence compression, grammatical function discrimination).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Use gaze as auxiliary signals; differ in tasks and modeling choices; limited prior NN-based learning from gaze compared to this paper's multimodal CNN.
comparable_works.source_trace: §8 Related Work paragraph referencing eye-tracking literature

comparable_works.relevance: Deep learning approaches to sarcasm detection combining RNNs and CNNs on text.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Focus on text-only deep models for sarcasm; this paper extends to incorporate cognitive gaze signals.

comparable_works.relevance: Guidance on statistical reporting, reproducibility, and reviewer conduct; relevant to flagged methodological reporting issues.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Not academic prior work but reviewer best-practices that recommend clear reporting, sharing of code/splits, and correct use of statistical tests.

uncertainty_flags: Statistical-test details sparse: no contingency tables, exact p-values, or multiple-comparison correction specified.
Participant-row ordering may be exploited; ordering invariance not tested.
Gaze preprocessing (min-max normalization) chosen without ablation; representation choices (word-id saccade encoding) not compared to alternatives.
Small number of readers per snippet (P=5–7) risks overfitting to reader idiosyncrasies; cross-subject generalization untested.
Hyperparameters selected by 'trial and error' and baseline tuning parity unclear; potential tuning bias.
Interpretability claim based on a few qualitative visualizations lacking quantitative metrics and confound controls (e.g., lexical differences).
alternative_interpretations: Activation differences attributed to gaze may be driven by lexical or syntactic differences between classes (especially given observed vocabulary separation in sarcasm dataset) rather than cognitive signals; thus gaze may be correlated but not causally informative.
Participant-order artifacts could explain apparent gains: if participant ordering correlates with data splits or label distributions, the model might learn a spurious ordering signal.
Normalization choices (min-max across participants) could remove inter-participant variance that is informative or introduce scale artifacts that favor particular model variants.

Apparent improvement over handcrafted baselines on dataset1 could be due to different preprocessing, embedding initializations, or hyperparameter choices rather than inherent superiority of learned gaze features.
transparency_notes: Authors claim use of same 10-fold configuration as prior works but do not provide fold indices or code; sharing these would greatly increase reproducibility.
Exact McNemar test application (which models compared, raw contingency counts) is not reported; authors should provide test data and predictions.
Gaze matrices, normalization scripts, and participant-ordering scheme are not included in the manuscript; releasing them would help verify representation-sensitive claims.
Hyperparameter selection process is described informally as 'trial and error'; a reproducible tuning log or fixed seed specification is missing.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The architectural idea of learning gaze features with CNNs and merging them with learned text features is relatively uncommon in the retrieved literature — this scarcity can indicate an innovative direction rather than a methodological error; however, novelty alone doesn't validate empirical claims, which require rigorous testing and controls.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If participant-ordering is shown not to influence performance (permutation-insensitive results), learned gaze features are more plausibly genuine cognitive signals.
If cross-subject generalization (leave-one-reader-out) holds with similar performance gains, the approach scales beyond idiosyncratic readers.
If normalization and alternate gaze encodings (z-score, per-word aggregation) yield consistent gains, the method is robust to preprocessing choices.
If quantitative separability of merge-layer activations persists after controlling for lexical cues, interpretability claims strengthen.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Applies established CNN techniques to a relatively under-explored modality (gaze) and demonstrates empirical gains on at least one public dataset; extends text CNNs with a concrete multimodal fusion design and variant studies.
evidence: Model integrates Kim (2014) style text CNN with 2D convolutions over P×G gaze matrices; empirical gains in Table 1 dataset1.
uncertainty_flags: Uncertainty about robustness due to limited statistical reporting, participant-order confound, and lack of cross-subject validation.

novelty_lenses.rationale: If confirmed and generalized, automatic learning of cognitive features from gaze could change how cognitive signals are integrated into NLP models (moving from hand-engineering to learned representations). However, disruptive impact depends on demonstrating robustness across datasets, readers, and preprocessing choices.
evidence: Gaze-only and combined models show nontrivial performance indicating that gaze carries signal; authors argue CNNs can discover features that handcrafted methods may miss.
uncertainty_flags: Dependence on small reader counts, dataset-specific results (dataset2 underperforms), and potential representation confounds reduces confidence in broad disruptive claims.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have medium confidence in the main directional findings (that learned gaze features can complement text and yield improvements on at least one dataset) because the manuscript provides direct empirical evidence (Tables 1–2) and acknowledges limitations. However, due to incomplete statistical reporting, potential confounds (participant ordering, preprocessing choices), small reader counts, and lack of quantitative interpretability analyses, the probability that the central claims fully generalize to other datasets and are free from methodological artifacts is substantially uncertain; hence a wide but centered interval.

consensus_findings: The manuscript proposes a clear multimodal CNN architecture that combines a Kim-style text CNN with a 2D-convolutional gaze branch (P×G matrices) and evaluates many variant configurations (text-only, gaze-only, combined) on two public gaze-enriched datasets.

On dataset1 (Mishra et al. 2016a) the reported combined text+gaze CNN variants achieve higher F-scores than the cited handcrafted text+gaze baselines, and the authors report that at least one of these improvements is statistically significant (McNemar p < 0.05).

Across the reported experiments, adding the learned gaze branch to text-only CNN variants yields consistent relative improvements in F-score versus the corresponding text-only CNNs, though effect sizes vary by dataset and task.

On dataset2 the CNN-based models underperform the best handcrafted-feature systems overall; authors report training behaviour (near-100% train accuracy with low validation) suggesting overfitting on that dataset.

Qualitative visualizations of merged hidden-layer activations are presented and interpreted as indicating that multimodal representations show pattern differences for sarcastic vs non-sarcastic examples, but the evidence is limited and anecdotal.
disagreements: Significance robustness: Reviewers agree a McNemar test was reported, but disagree about whether the statistical evidence as presented is sufficient—some treat the reported p-value as provisional evidence contingent on disclosure of contingency tables and multiple-comparison control, while others emphasize the lack of exact statistics undermines confidence.

Interpretability strength: Reviewers concur the visualizations are interesting; some characterize them as hypothesis-generating only (insufficient to support strong interpretability claims), while one reviewer is more optimistic about their indicative value provided further quantitative analyses are added.

Novelty assessment: Reviewers uniformly note architectural novelty relative to handcrafted-feature prior work, but differ on magnitude — some label it 'moderately novel' or 'meaningful incremental advance', others frame it as a potentially disruptive framing if methodological gaps are addressed.

Severity of methodological gaps: All reviewers flag methodological concerns (statistical reporting, participant-order dependence, preprocessing choices, hyperparameter tuning, small reader counts). They differ slightly in emphasis: some prioritize the participant-ordering confound as a major threat, others prioritize reproducibility materials and statistical details as the primary blockers to validation.
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical reporting: absence of contingency tables, exact p-values, and no described correction for multiple pairwise comparisons across many model variants.

Participant-order sensitivity: the gaze P×G encoding is order-sensitive and the manuscript keeps a fixed row order without experiments that randomize rows or adopt permutation-invariant pooling — potential for spurious ordering signals.

Gaze preprocessing choices: reliance on min-max normalization across participants and the chosen saccade representations without ablation to z-score, per-participant standardization, per-word aggregation, or randomized-noise controls.

Small per-snippet reader counts (P=5 or 7): risk that learned gaze features capture reader-specific idiosyncrasies rather than general cognitive patterns; cross-subject generalization tests (leave-one-reader-out, held-out readers) are missing.

Baseline/hyperparameter parity: hyperparameters reportedly chosen 'by trial and error' and no systematic hyperparameter search is documented, raising the possibility that variant comparisons reflect tuning differences rather than model-level effects.

Interpretability claims: merge-layer visualization evidence is qualitative and limited to a few examples; no quantitative separability metrics or ablations controlling for lexical confounds are provided.
model_diversity_effects: Comparisons across many model variants (text-static, text-nonstatic, multichannel text, fixation/saccade/multichannel gaze, and their combinations) reveal a consistent pattern: combined text+gaze CNNs improve over corresponding text-only CNNs, suggesting the learned gaze branch adds complementary signal when held in the same architecture family.

However, the relative performance of CNNs versus prior handcrafted systems is dataset-dependent: on dataset1 the learned multimodal approach outperforms prior handcrafted baselines, while on dataset2 the handcrafted systems still lead. This model-dataset interaction implies that dataset characteristics (size, reader heterogeneity, text genre) modulate whether learned gaze representations are advantageous.

Because participant-ordering, preprocessing, and hyperparameter choices were kept constant across many variants, some of the measured improvements may be persistent across variants but still vulnerable to the same shared biases; diversity of model variants does not by itself eliminate representation or dataset confounds.

Gaze-only variants produce nontrivial but lower performance than combined models, indicating that gaze encodes task-relevant signal but is insufficient alone for top performance on the evaluated tasks.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the paper as presenting a promising architectural direction (learning gaze features via CNNs) with empirical support on at least one public dataset, but with several methodological/reporting deficiencies that merit remediation before strong claims are accepted as robust. Central editorial actions: (1) Request that authors supply reproducibility artifacts (code, exact 10-fold split indices, random seeds, preprocessing scripts, and processed gaze matrices). (2) Require authors to provide full statistical test details (contingency tables for McNemar tests, exact p-values) and to state how multiple comparisons were handled or to apply appropriate corrections. (3) Ask for targeted additional experiments addressing the top uncertainty hotspots: permutation tests or permutation-invariant aggregation for participant rows, normalization ablations (min-max vs z-score vs per-participant), and cross-subject generalization (leave-one-reader-out). (4) Request quantitative analyses for the interpretability claim (separability/clustering metrics on merge-layer activations, probe classifiers, and lexical-confound controls). (5) Ask for documentation of hyperparameter search or at least sensitivity analyses and assurance of fair tuning of baselines. Position the editor as decision arbiter: these remediation items should be required for claims to be considered fully substantiated in editorial communications and for downstream reviewers to reassess evidence strength.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript's evidential basis, provide the following: (1) Reproducibility materials: release code, preprocessing scripts to build P×G gaze matrices, exact train/validation/test fold indices (the 10-fold splits), random seeds, and representative processed gaze files (or deterministic reconstruction scripts if raw gaze data cannot be shared). (2) Statistical transparency: for each claimed significant pairwise comparison, release the contingency table (counts of instances where model A correct/B incorrect and vice versa), exact p-values, and state whether and how you correct for multiple comparisons (or predefine a primary comparison and report corrected p-values). (3) Participant-order robustness: run experiments that (a) randomly permute participant row orders across training and test to assess sensitivity, and (b) implement permutation-invariant alternatives (mean/max pooling across participants, attention-based pooling, or DeepSets-style processing) and report results. (4) Preprocessing ablations: compare min-max vs z-score vs per-participant standardization, test per-word aggregated gaze statistics vs sequence representations, and report performance and stability. (5) Cross-subject generalization: perform leave-one-reader-out or held-out-reader experiments to quantify dependence on specific readers. (6) Interpretability quantification: compute separability/clustering metrics (silhouette, cluster purity, or classification accuracy using merge-layer features), probe whether activations correlate with simple lexical features, and run a shuffled-gaze control (assign gaze from other snippets) to check signal vs artifact. (7) Hyperparameter fairness: document the hyperparameter search (ranges, selection criteria) and ensure baselines received comparable tuning; report sensitivity analyses or confidence intervals over multiple seeds/folds. (8) Provide learning curves (train/validation loss and accuracy) for key datasets/variants to substantiate overfitting statements. Addressing these points will materially reduce key uncertainties and make empirical claims more robust.
transparency_report: What is present: clear architectural descriptions (text and gaze branches), lists of fixed hyperparameters used during training, detailed result tables across many model variants, and candid acknowledgement of some limitations (dataset dependence, participant-ordering awareness, need for more tuning).

What is missing and requested: code and preprocessing scripts, exact 10-fold split indices and random seeds, processed P×G gaze matrices (or scripts to build them), contingency tables and exact p-values for statistical tests, learning curves for train/validation, and logs of hyperparameter selection. Without these artifacts, independent reproducibility and verification of statistical claims are impeded.

Minimal deliverables recommended for transparency: (a) a public repository with code and scripts; (b) a data README describing gaze encoding and participant ordering used; (c) a table or file with model predictions per test fold so reviewers can reconstruct McNemar tests and other paired comparisons.
epistemic_limits: The synthesis is constrained by reliance on the manuscript's reported numbers, descriptions, and reviewers' reconstructions; I have not executed the experiments nor examined raw model outputs or original gaze logs. Observed reported improvements (e.g., +3.8% F on dataset1) are taken at face value but their robustness depends on undisclosed details (exact splits, preprocessing, and statistical contingency counts). Interpretability inferences based on a few visualizations are intrinsically weak without quantitative validation; thus any strong inference that the model captures cognitive processes should be treated as provisional. Finally, small reader counts and order-sensitive gaze encodings constitute structural limitations that cannot be fully resolved by reading alone — empirical permutation and cross-subject tests are needed to reduce uncertainty. All recommendations assume authors are able to run the additional ablations and release artifacts; absent this, the evidential status of the claims remains uncertain.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript introduces a multimodal CNN that jointly learns features from text and multi-reader eye-movement (gaze) inputs (encoded as P×G matrices processed by 2D convolutions) and evaluates many variants (text-only, gaze-only, combined) on two public gaze-enriched datasets for sentiment polarity and sarcasm detection. Reported results show that combined text+gaze CNN variants outperform corresponding text-only CNNs across variants and that, on dataset1, a combined variant attains higher F-score than a cited handcrafted text+gaze baseline (reported max +3.8% F; McNemar p < 0.05). On dataset2, CNNs underperform the best handcrafted system overall, though adding gaze still improves text-only CNNs; training dynamics on dataset2 suggest overfitting. The manuscript also presents qualitative visualizations of merged hidden-layer activations to argue that the learned multimodal representations differ for sarcastic vs non-sarcastic examples. Reviewers find the architectural framing and empirical direction promising but identify important methodological, statistical, and reproducibility gaps that limit confidence in the robustness and generality of the claims.
strengths: Clear multimodal architecture: integrates a Kim (2014)-style text CNN with a 2D-convolutional gaze branch over P×G matrices and reports numerous ablation-like variant comparisons (static/non-static/multichannel text × fixation/saccade/multichannel gaze).
Empirical evaluation on two public gaze-enriched datasets, enabling comparisons with prior handcrafted text+gaze baselines (e.g., Mishra et al. 2016) and exposing dataset-dependent effects.

Honest reporting of limitations and dataset dependence: authors note cases where CNNs underperform (dataset2), observe suspicious training/validation behavior, and discuss representation and hyperparameter concerns.
limitations: Incomplete statistical reporting: statistical-significance claims cite McNemar p < 0.05 but do not provide contingency tables, exact p-values, which pairwise comparisons were tested, nor any multiple-comparison correction. This prevents independent verification of claimed significance.

Participant-order confound in gaze encoding: gaze is encoded as P×G matrices with a fixed row ordering of participants; the model is order-sensitive and the manuscript does not report permutation tests or permutation-invariant alternatives, so ordering artifacts could drive results.

Gaze preprocessing and representation choices under-validated: min-max normalization across participants and the chosen saccade encodings are used without ablation against z-score, per-participant standardization, per-word aggregation, or shuffled-gaze controls, leaving robustness uncertain.

Small per-snippet reader counts and lack of cross-subject tests: datasets use P=7 and P=5 readers per snippet; no leave-one-reader-out or held-out-reader experiments are reported to assess whether learned features generalize beyond specific readers.
open_questions: Please provide the contingency tables (counts where model A correct & B incorrect and vice versa), exact p-values, and specify which pairwise comparisons were tested with McNemar; how were multiple comparisons handled (if at all)?

How sensitive are results to participant-row ordering? Please report experiments that (a) randomly permute participant rows (train and test) and (b) implement a permutation-invariant alternative (e.g., per-participant encoding + mean/max pooling or attention) and compare performance.

What preprocessing scripts and exact 10-fold split indices were used? Please release code or scripts (or, if data-sharing restricted, deterministic reconstruction scripts) so reported numbers can be reproduced exactly.

Please report ablation experiments for gaze normalization (min-max vs z-score vs per-participant standardization), for saccade encoding variants (direction/length vs word-id sequences), and a shuffled-gaze control (assign gaze matrices to unrelated snippets) to quantify signal vs artifact.
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers agree the paper presents a coherent multimodal CNN architecture and a comprehensive set of model variants evaluated on two public gaze-enriched datasets.
All reviewers observe consistent relative improvements when adding the learned gaze branch to text-only CNN variants across the reported experiments.
All reviewers flag the dataset-dependent nature of gains: improvements over handcrafted baselines are reported on dataset1 but not on dataset2, and authors acknowledge overfitting signs on dataset2.
All reviewers request reproducibility artifacts (code, exact split indices, preprocessing scripts) and stronger statistical reporting and ablation studies to substantiate robustness claims.
disagreement_snapshot: Magnitude of evidential sufficiency: reviewers concur the reported numerical improvements are promising, but they differ in their readiness to treat the reported McNemar p-value as convincing absent contingency tables and multiple-comparison correction — ranging from provisional acceptance to substantial skepticism.

Interpretability weight: reviewers uniformly see Figure 4 visualizations as hypothesis-generating; some are cautiously optimistic that more quantitative analysis would validate the interpretability claim, while others treat the current qualitative evidence as too weak to support claims about cognitive-signal capture.

Novelty framing: reviewers agree on conceptual novelty (end-to-end learned gaze features) but vary on labeling it incremental vs potentially disruptive—this hinges on whether methodological gaps (ordering, generalization) can be closed.
uncertainty_snapshot: Statistical uncertainty: Without contingency tables and multiple-test adjustments, significance labels (p < 0.05) possess unclear Type I error risk across many pairwise comparisons.
Representation uncertainty: Without permutation/aggregation experiments, it is unknown whether the model learns participant-agnostic cognitive patterns or exploits ordering/reader-id artifacts.

Generalization uncertainty: Given small P and absence of cross-subject validation, it is unknown whether learned gaze features generalize to unseen readers or to datasets with different reader composition.

Interpretability uncertainty: Qualitative activation plots lack quantitative separability metrics and confound controls (lexical overlap, length), so attribution to cognitive processes remains provisional.
source_trace: Kim (2014) sentence-level CNN architecture used for text component (manuscript §4.1; reviewers reference Kim 2014).
Mishra et al. (2016b/c) handcrafted text+gaze baselines and dataset1 comparisons reported in manuscript Table 1 and §6.1 (reviewers repeatedly reference these comparisons).
Joshi et al. (2014/2015) and other sarcasm/sentiment baseline references for dataset2 and Table 2 (manuscript §5 and §6.2; reviewers reference these works).
Manuscript §4.2 describing gaze P×G representation and statement that gaze branch is not invariant to participant row order (reviewers cite this as a key methodological assumption).
Manuscript §6.1 reporting training dynamics for dataset2 (training accuracy ~100% within 25 epochs while validation ~50%), used by reviewers to infer overfitting risk.

Manuscript Figure 4 and §7 qualitative visualization of merged 150-d hidden-layer activations for a few sarcastic/non-sarcastic examples (reviewers note qualitative nature and request quantitative separability metrics).
transparency_notes: Manuscript provides detailed architecture descriptions, hyperparameters used, and per-variant result tables, and it candidly acknowledges several limitations. Missing or insufficiently reported items that constrain verification: code and preprocessing scripts (for constructing P×G gaze matrices), exact 10-fold split indices and random seeds, model prediction outputs per test fold (needed to reconstruct McNemar contingency tables), and detailed statistical-test outputs (exact p-values and multiple-comparison handling). Providing these artifacts would materially increase reproducibility and statistical credibility.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the submission as a promising contribution that advances an architectural framing (learned gaze features via CNNs) but one that requires targeted methodological and reporting remediation before its empirical claims can be judged robust. Request authors to: (1) release code and preprocessing scripts plus exact 10-fold split indices and random seeds (or provide deterministic reconstruction scripts if raw gaze logs cannot be shared); (2) supply contingency tables and exact p-values for all claimed McNemar tests and describe how multiple comparisons were handled or apply corrections; (3) run and report permutation/aggregation experiments to address participant-order sensitivity (random row permutations, and a permutation-invariant pooling/attention alternative); (4) perform preprocessing ablations (min-max vs z-score vs per-participant standardization, per-word aggregated gaze features, shuffled-gaze control); (5) run cross-subject generalization tests (leave-one-reader-out or held-out-reader evaluations); (6) add quantitative analyses supporting interpretability claims (separability/clustering metrics and lexical-confound checks); (7) document hyperparameter search/tuning procedures and ensure fairness of baseline tuning; (8) include learning curves for train/validation to substantiate overfitting claims. These deliverables should be requested prior to revising the manuscript’s core empirical claims.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidential support and reduce uncertainty, provide: (1) reproducibility artifacts — public code repository, preprocessing scripts to build P×G gaze matrices, exact train/validation/test fold indices for the 10-fold splits, and random seeds (or deterministic reconstruction scripts if privacy restricts sharing raw gaze); (2) statistical transparency — contingency tables for each McNemar comparison, exact p-values, and statement of multiple-comparison corrections (or pre-specify primary comparisons); (3) participant-order robustness tests — results for randomized participant-row orders and for permutation-invariant aggregation (per-participant encoders + mean/max pooling or attention/DeepSets architectures); (4) preprocessing ablations — compare min-max vs z-score vs per-participant normalization, test per-word aggregated gaze statistics versus time-sequence encodings, and include a shuffled-gaze control to measure chance effects; (5) cross-subject generalization — leave-one-reader-out or held-out-reader experiments to quantify dependence on specific readers; (6) interpretability quantification — compute separability/clustering metrics (silhouette, ARI, classification probes on merge-layer features), and test correlations with simple lexical features and controls that mask top discriminative words; (7) hyperparameter-sensitivity documentation — provide hyperparameter search ranges, validation selection procedures, and ensure baselines receive comparable tuning; (8) learning curves and training/validation loss/accuracy traces for key variants. Addressing these items will materially reduce the main epistemic uncertainties.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The manuscript proposes a multimodal CNN that jointly learns features from text and multi-reader gaze inputs (encoded as P×G matrices and processed by 2D convolutions). Evaluations on two public gaze-enriched datasets show that adding learned gaze features consistently improves text-only CNN variants and that on dataset1 a combined model outperforms a cited handcrafted text+gaze baseline (reported +3.8% F, McNemar p < 0.05). On dataset2 CNNs underperform the best handcrafted systems and show signs consistent with overfitting. The paper includes qualitative visualizations of merge-layer activations to argue the learned multimodal representations capture distinctions relevant to sarcasm.

Strengths:
- Clear, reproducible-seeming architecture that extends standard text CNNs with a 2D gaze branch and reports many variant combinations (text/gaze channel ablations).
- Empirical evaluation on two public datasets, facilitating comparability and exposing dataset-specific behavior.
- Candid discussion of some limitations (dataset dependence, overfitting on dataset2, representation ordering sensitivity).

Limitations:
- Missing statistical detail: McNemar p-values are reported but contingency tables, exact p-values, and multiple-comparison handling are absent; this prevents independent verification of significance claims.

Open Questions:
- Please provide contingency tables and exact p-values for McNemar tests; which pairwise comparisons were tested and how were multiple comparisons corrected?
- How does randomizing participant row order affect results, and how do permutation-invariant pooling/attention variants perform relative to the current ordering-sensitive architecture?
- Can you release the preprocessing scripts, exact 10-fold split indices, and random seeds (or deterministic reconstruction scripts) so reported results can be exactly reproduced?
- What is the effect of alternative gaze normalizations (min-max vs z-score vs per-participant standardization) and of a shuffled-gaze control on reported gains?

The manuscript provides detailed architecture descriptions, hyperparameter lists, and per-variant results, and it acknowledges limitations. Missing items that are critical for reproducibility and verification include: code and preprocessing scripts to build P×G gaze matrices, exact 10-fold split indices and seeds, per-fold model predictions (for reconstructing contingency tables), and detailed statistical outputs. Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Write the review you would like to get yourself. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.
